title: Wontons in Chilli Oil
subtitle: Boiled pork wontons tossed in a tangy garlic and chilli oil sauce
excerpt: Pork wontons are folded in thin commercial wrappers, boiled until silky and then dressed in a sauce of chilli oil, black vinegar, soy sauce and garlic. The result is sharp, oily, warming and completely addictive. Serves 4 in about 50 minutes.
sourceNotes: Wontons in spiced oil or broth are a staple of Sichuan street food, documented in detail in Fuchsia Dunlop's 'Land of Plenty' (Michael Joseph, 2001), which remains the most authoritative English-language treatment of Sichuan home cooking. The dish is also discussed in Yan-Kit So's 'Classic Food of China' (Macmillan, 1992), which traces the wonton's origins to northern wheat-flour traditions that spread southward along trade routes.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze uncooked wontons on a lined tray until solid, then transfer to a bag for up to 3 months. Boil from frozen for 6 to 7 minutes, adding an extra minute or two.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The filling can be made a day ahead and kept in the fridge. The sauce can be mixed and kept at room temperature for up to 2 days.

glossaryTerms.definition: Thin squares of egg-enriched wheat dough, sold fresh or frozen in Chinese grocery shops. They are thinner and more elastic than dumpling skins and turn silky when boiled. Square wrappers are used for wontons; round wrappers are usually for gyoza-style dumplings.

Oil infused with dried chillies, often with aromatics such as Sichuan pepper, star anise and garlic added during cooking. Good chilli oil has a deep red colour and a layered heat that builds slowly. Chinese chilli oil (la jiao you) differs from Southeast Asian varieties in its drier, more fragrant character.

The dried husks of the prickly ash berry, not a true peppercorn. They produce a numbing, tingling sensation on the tongue called ma, which is a defining feature of Sichuan cuisine. They are sold whole or ground and should be toasted briefly before use to develop their floral aroma.

A dark, mellow Chinese vinegar made from fermented grains, most commonly associated with Zhenjiang in Jiangsu province. It has a complex, slightly smoky flavour that is less sharp than rice vinegar and works well in sauces and dressings. Balsamic vinegar is not a substitute; use rice vinegar if black vinegar is unavailable.

content.text: This recipe serves 4 and takes about 50 minutes, including folding roughly 30 wontons. The sauce comes together in 5 minutes, so it is worth making the sauce first and setting it aside while you fold and cook. The finished dish is best eaten straight away while the wontons are still hot and the dressing is glossy.

are optional but give the sauce a characteristic numbing warmth that is worth seeking out.

Mix the {{pork-mince}}, {{spring-onions}}, {{ginger}}, {{soy-sauce}}, {{sesame-oil}} and white pepper together in a bowl. Stir in one direction only for about a minute to build a slightly springy texture. Cover and chill while you make the sauce.
Whisk together the {{chilli-oil}}, {{soy-sauce}}, {{black-vinegar}}, {{garlic}}, {{sesame-oil}}, {{sugar}} and ground Sichuan peppercorns if using. Taste and adjust. Set aside.

Set out the {{wonton-wrappers}} with a small bowl of water nearby. Place a rounded teaspoon of filling in the centre of a wrapper. Dip a finger in water and wet two adjacent edges. Fold the wrapper in half diagonally to form a triangle, pressing out air and sealing firmly. Bring the two far corners of the triangle together, wet one corner and press to join. Repeat with the remaining wrappers and filling.

Bring a large pot of water to a rolling boil. Add the wontons in two or three batches to avoid crowding. Cook for 4 to 5 minutes, stirring gently once, until they float and the skins look translucent. Lift out with a slotted spoon and drain briefly.
Divide the sauce between four bowls. Add the hot wontons, toss gently and top with sliced spring onions. Serve immediately.

items.symptom: Wontons are bursting open during boiling
items.cause: Filling is overfilled or the seal was not pressed firmly
items.fix: Use no more than a rounded teaspoon of filling. Press all air out before sealing and check each wonton is properly closed before it goes in the water.

items.symptom: Wrappers are sticking together before cooking
items.cause: They were left uncovered or stacked without separation
items.fix: Dust folded wontons lightly with cornflour and keep them on a tray covered with a damp cloth until ready to boil.

items.cause: The chilli oil lacks sediment or the vinegar was left out
items.fix: Use chilli oil that includes the red sediment at the bottom of the jar, which carries most of the flavour. Add the black vinegar a little at a time and taste as you go.

content.text: Wontons dressed in chilli oil are most closely associated with Sichuan street food, where vendors sell bowls of them from carts with an array of condiments on the side. The Cantonese version, served in a clear broth, is a separate but related dish. This Sichuan preparation is saucier, bolder and better suited to a weeknight dinner at home. The
does almost all the work once folded, and the sauce takes minutes to put together.
